title: John Henry Newman (1801–1890)
hook: an Oxford Anglican priest becomes Catholic, and the Church later names him a saint

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauline Jaricot and her circles of givers. Your line was small groups, whole world. Where did your coin go? Today, a man on a becalmed ship, and the end of a week. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

A sailing ship, stuck. No wind. The sea is flat, and the boat sits there, going nowhere. On board is a young English clergyman who has nearly died of a fever in Sicily. He wants badly to be home; he believes there is work waiting for him there, though he cannot see what it is. So, with nothing to do and nowhere to go, he writes a short poem. It begins with three words, and it asks for very little: not a map, not the whole road. Just enough light for the next step. People still sing it as a hymn.
screen: `A SHIP WITH NO WIND.` → `FAR FROM HOME, AND ILL.` → `A SHORT POEM ON BOARD.`

segments.voice: The clergyman was John Henry Newman. Four chapters in his life. First, Oxford. Newman was a priest of the Church of England, a fellow of an Oxford college and a preacher at the university church, and his sermons drew students in. He and his friends set out to recover the Church of England's roots in the early Church, and he read the early Christian writers closely. Second, the turn. The deeper he read, the more he became convinced that the Catholic Church was the Church of those early writers. He was received into the Catholic Church. It cost him his post, his place at Oxford and many old friendships, and he wrote that it felt like coming into port after a rough sea. Third, the poem from the ship. Newman wrote: "Lead, Kindly Light, amid the encircling gloom, Lead Thou me on! The night is dark, and I am far from home; Lead Thou me on!" And then the line people remember: "Keep Thou my feet; I do not ask to see The distant scene; one step enough for me." He wrote it years before his conversion. It is a prayer for someone who does not know where they are going. Fourth, the saint. Newman spent his Catholic years as a priest of the Oratory in Birmingham, writing, teaching, and looking after a parish, and late in life the pope made him a cardinal. The Church has since canonized him. Anglicans honor him too, and both still sing his poem. The man who asked for one step got a long road, one step at a time.
screen: `AN OXFORD PREACHER.` · `RECEIVED INTO THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.` · `ONE STEP ENOUGH FOR ME.` · `A PRIEST, A CARDINAL, A SAINT.` · then, large: `LEAD, KINDLY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray lead, kindly light, or simply sit with it. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your life where you can't see the distant scene. A decision. A worry. A road with no map. Don't try to solve it. Ask only for the next step. If you pray, you can say Newman's words slowly: lead, kindly light, lead thou me on. If you don't, just hold the phrase one step enough, and see what the next small step might be. The bell holds the time.
Oratory. The community in Birmingham where John Henry Newman spent his Catholic years as a priest, writing, teaching, and looking after a parish.

Your line: lead, kindly light. This week: light through a window on a tax collector, towns built with the Guaraní, the passion remembered, a Church always renewing, a priest in the confessional, small circles of givers, and now one step at a time. Today, take one next step on something you can't see the end of. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint John Henry Newman's feast on October 9, and his poem Lead, Kindly Light is sung as a hymn in Catholic and Anglican churches and at funerals.

fork.setup: you are a respected Oxford preacher, and your reading of the early Church leads you toward the Catholic Church. what do you do?
options: stay quiet and keep your post.
become Catholic, knowing it will cost your place and friends.
fork.reveal: Newman was received into the Catholic Church. it cost him his post at Oxford and many friendships.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lead, Kindly Light is a hymn written for a church service.
what it means: it began as a short poem Newman wrote on a becalmed ship, far from home and recovering from illness, asking for one step's worth of light.
what a scholar hears: Newman titled the poem The Pillar of the Cloud, after the cloud that led Israel through the desert, and he wrote it as an Anglican.
